pages.x: Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith who could not read any language, spent years working out a sign for each syllable of his own. When he showed his system in 1821 it was so easy that thousands of Cherokee learned to read and write within a few years, and in 1828 they began a newspaper printed in it.

The southeast was still home to the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Chickasaw, Choctaw and Seminole nations. The Cherokee had a written constitution and a capital at New Echota in Georgia; many farmed, and some ran plantations worked by enslaved Black people. Then in 1829 gold was found on their land, and settlers poured in.

President Andrew Jackson, who had made his name fighting the Creek, wanted all the nations moved west of the Mississippi. In 1830 Congress passed the Indian Removal Act by a handful of votes. The Choctaw were moved first, in winters so cruel that one of their chiefs called it a trail of tears and death.

The Cherokee fought in the courts, and in 1832 the Supreme Court ruled that Georgia had no power over their land. Georgia ignored it, and Jackson did nothing to make it obey. In 1835 a small group of Cherokee signed away the nation's land at New Echota; the chief, John Ross, and most of his people never agreed.

In 1838 soldiers rounded up some 16,000 Cherokee into camps, then sent them more than 1,500 kilometres west through autumn and winter, many on foot. Sickness, cold and hunger killed thousands on the way, the old and the young hardest of all. The Cherokee remember it as the trail where they cried.

The survivors rebuilt in Indian Territory, now Oklahoma, and in 1839 made Tahlequah their capital. In Florida the Seminole fought removal in long wars, and some were never moved. By 1850 most of the southeast's Native people had been driven west, and their land had gone to white settlers, much of it for cotton grown by enslaved people.

About 60,000 people of the five nations were forced from their homes, in one of the darkest chapters of American history. The Cherokee Nation rebuilt in Oklahoma, and today it is the largest tribe in the United States, still governed from Tahlequah, where children learn to read in Sequoyah's letters.
